_comment: #823(d) — the CROSS-LANGUAGE contract for the range matcher.
Two implementations resolve a cell against a band list: Python's
from apply, derive and a grid edit) and TypeScript's
#542b is the standing record of what a second implementation costs here:
one cell got two different numbers depending on which path computed it. A
table in each suite would drift silently the first time somebody fixed one
side; both suites execute THIS file, so a divergence fails in whichever
`expected: null` means no band matched. The Python side reads null as None
and the TS side as undefined — those are each language's 'no match', and
each suite asserts its own spelling.

cases.name: inclusive at the low bound
inclusive at the high bound
just past the high bound
an open top is unbounded
an open bottom is unbounded
first declared band wins on overlap
the later band still matches outside the earlier one
a thousands separator parses the same on both sides
surrounding whitespace is trimmed
a non-numeric cell matches nothing
an EMPTY cell is not zero
a whitespace-only cell is not zero either
part-numeric text matches nothing
a negative value lands in a negative band
a decimal lands in its band
a numeric output survives as a number
no bands means no match

_comment: #862 — the glyph and radix cases. The table above carried NO
glyph-bearing cell, so both suites passed while the client stripped
commas and nothing else: measured across 39 inputs, 16 disagreed, and
every currency and percent cell was one of them — on exactly the column
types a researcher bands. These are the cases that fail in whichever
cases.name: a currency cell bands by its number
a percent cell bands by its FACE value, not by hundredths
a euro sign is stripped like a dollar sign
a pound sign is stripped like a dollar sign
a yen sign is stripped like a dollar sign
a glyph is removed ANYWHERE, not only at the ends
a sign SURVIVES the glyph strip
a hex literal is NOT a number — the client used to say 16
a binary literal is not a number either
an underscore between digits parses, as float() allows
a doubled underscore does not
an exponent parses on both sides
a bare sign is not a number
